Hackles are the hairs (or feathers, in birds) that run along the back of the neck — and sometimes down the spine — of certain animals. Think of a dog, a cat, a wolf, or a rooster. That strip of fur or feathers sitting on the back of their neck? That's the hackles.

The most important thing to understand about hackles is what they do: they stand up and bristle when the animal is angry, scared, or feeling threatened. You've probably seen a dog's fur spike up along its neck when it senses danger — that's the hackles rising. A rooster fluffs up the feathers around its neck when it's about to fight — same thing.

So in its most literal sense, hackles = the fur or feathers on the back of the neck/spine that rise up as a physical sign of alarm, aggression, or tension.

• Dogs and wolves: A ridge of stiff fur rises from the neck down toward the shoulders. This is often the clearest and most famous example.
  • Cats: Similar raised fur along the spine and neck — this is why an alarmed cat looks like it suddenly doubled in size.
  • Roosters and fighting birds: The long, flowing feathers around the neck flare outward dramatically. In fact, these neck feathers on a rooster are called hackles specifically, even when they're not raised. Fly fishermen actually use rooster hackle feathers to tie artificial fishing flies.
The Figurative Meaning (How It Applies to People)

This is where the word becomes truly useful in everyday English, because people use "hackles" to describe human anger and irritation too — through a handful of very common phrases.

The idea is borrowed from animals: just as a dog's hackles rise when it feels threatened or provoked, a person's metaphorical hackles rise when they feel annoyed, defensive, or angry.

"To raise someone's hackles"

This is the single most common phrase. It means to annoy, irritate, or offend someone — to provoke a defensive or angry reaction in them.

"His rude tone immediately raised her hackles."
(= His rudeness made her feel irritated and defensive.)

"That politician's speech raised hackles across the country."
(= It angered and offended many people.)

"Someone's hackles rose / are up"

This describes the state of being already annoyed or ready to react aggressively.

"His hackles rose the moment they walked into the room."
(= He immediately became tense, wary, and irritated.)

"She walked into the meeting with her hackles up."
(= She was already defensive and on edge before anything even happened.)

"With hackles raised"

Used to describe someone who is visibly agitated, defensive, or ready to argue.

"He responded to the criticism with hackles raised."
(= He replied in an angry, defensive manner.)

Whether you're talking about an animal or a person, hackles are always about threat, tension, and defensive aggression. The image is the same: something provokes a reaction, and the body (literally or figuratively) bristles in response. The raised hackles of a growling dog is the perfect physical picture of what the word always means, even when used about humans.

LiterallyThe fur/feathers on the back of an animal's neck that bristle when the animal is threatened or aggressive
FigurativelyUsed in phrases to describe human irritation, anger, or defensiveness
Key phrase"raise someone's hackles" = to irritate or offend someone
Core feelingThreat → tension → bristling defensiveness
One Sentence to Remember It Forever

Hackles are the hairs on the back of a dog's neck that stand up when it's ready to growl — and in everyday English, "raising someone's hackles" means making them feel that same bristling, defensive irritation.
